item.title: Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education
item.description:
Educational Technology Research and Development
Abstract Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly framed as a catalyst for deeper learning rather than simple automation. This design-based study investigated how personalised GPT agents were used as cognitive partners by pre-service teachers in an undergraduate Initial Teacher Education course in Digital Technologies within a Bachelor of Education (Secondary) programme. Drawing on distributed cognition, constructivism, cognitive load theory, and critical AI literacy, the intervention embedded personalised GPT agents within a university Canvas Learning Management System. Fourteen students configured and used agents aligned to curriculum goals, teaching contexts, pedagogical preferences, and weekly Prompt–Reflect–Refine tasks. Data included approximately 7,000 AI interactions, reflective journals, assessed lesson and assessment artefacts, and tutorial-group discussions. A hybrid inductive–deductive thematic analysis identified four recurrent functions in students’ use of the agents: conceptual tutor, co-designer, reflective mirror, and cognitive challenger. Across data sources, students reported clearer conceptual support, iterative planning, and reflective prompting, alongside risks of over-reliance, factual drift, and culturally narrow exemplars. The study contributes a context-specific model for LMS-integrated generative AI that foregrounds partnership, personalisation, judgement, and ethical reflexivity. Findings should be interpreted cautiously because the study was small-scale, single-site, and partly reliant on self-reported reflection.

item.title: AI Ingratiation in Content Generation: A Dual-Pathway Model of Intimacy and Authenticity
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in content generation, understanding how its interaction styles shape user responses is critical. This study examines AI ingratiation—AI-generated expressions of praise and flattery—and its effects on user perceptions and behavioral outcomes. A 2×2 online experiment reveals that AI ingratiation increases perceived intimacy but decreases perceived authenticity. Building on these perceptual responses, perceived intimacy and perceived authenticity jointly transmit the effects of AI ingratiation to user satisfaction and content iteration intention, indicating significant indirect effects through these dual mediating pathways. We further examine the moderating role of AI literacy and find that users with higher self-reported AI usage literacy are more responsive to AI ingratiation. Specifically, higher AI literacy strengthens the positive effect of AI ingratiation on perceived intimacy, which in turn enhances user satisfaction. Finally, a multi-group analysis reveals significant differences between advertising and academic contexts, suggesting that the effects of AI ingratiation vary across content generation scenarios. These findings highlight the dual-pathway and context-dependent nature of AI ingratiation in human–AI interaction.

item.title: Unpacking the Experience Economy of Role-Playing Conversational AI: A Grounded Theory Analysis
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
The rapid rise of role-playing conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed human-AI interaction from task-oriented exchanges into immersive, scenario-based digital experiences. However, while prior studies predominantly evaluate AI through utilitarian performance or relational support, the holistic experiential structure of these novel interactions remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, this paper draws on the experience economy (4Es) framework to investigate how users experience role-playing conversational AI through the realms of entertainment, education, esthetics, and escapism. Using a grounded theory approach, this study analyzes 6,171 user comments from the Reddit community r/CharacterAI. Findings reveal that user-AI role-playing is fundamentally multidimensional: entertainment and escapism emerge as particularly salient, while educational and esthetic experiences are also clearly present. Ultimately, this study extends the 4Es framework into the context of generative AI, offering a foundational empirical understanding of this emerging form of experiential consumption.

item.title: Trust in AI-Assisted Newsvendor Decisions: Effects of Information Design
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
As artificial-intelligence-assisted tools become prevalent in supply chain inventory management, algorithmic trust critically determines the success of human-AI interaction. Based on the newsvendor decision making, this study primarily considers two key factors—information construal level and presentation format—to investigate how they affect trust in AI recommendation, alongside the moderating role of decision-makers' individual traits. Through an incentivized 2×3 between-subjects experiment, we empirically analyze the level of trust in AI decision-making tools, measured by participants' Mean Absolute Percentage Deviation (MAPD) from the AI-advised values across different groups. Results indicate that text-and-graphic and scenario-based presentation formats significantly reduce decision deviation and enhance AI trust, whereas the construal level shows no significant impact. Furthermore, while decision-making style significantly influences AI tool utilization frequency, it does not affect the actual adoption of AI advice. This study clarifies the mechanisms driving algorithmic trust in newsvendor settings and provides empirical evidence and guidelines for enterprises to optimize the front-end interactive design of AI decision assistants and implement differentiated promotion and literacy training strategies tailored to varying employee traits.

item.title: The Paradox of Efficiency: Teacher-Directed AI Misuse and the Burden of Busywork in Higher Education
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into higher education to enhance instructional efficiency and improve learning outcomes. However, its adoption has revealed a paradox: AI-enabled teaching may unintentionally increase student workload without corresponding educational benefits. This study examines teacher-generated “algorithmic busywork,” defined as excessive, low-value assignments produced using Artificial intelligence tools with limited pedagogical design. Using survey data from 206 undergraduate students across multiple universities, we analyze students’ exposure to AI-generated assignments, their perceived educational value, and associated cognitive and emotional responses. The findings indicate that AI misuse in teaching is linked to increased academic stress, reduced engagement, and perceived inefficiencies in learning. Many students report that AI-generated tasks are repetitive, weakly aligned with learning objectives, and detract from more meaningful learning activities.This study contributes to the information systems and digital education literature by shifting attention from student misuse to teacher-directed Artificial intelligence practices. It highlights the need for pedagogical guidelines to ensure that AI-enabled teaching improves, rather than undermines, student outcomes.

item.title: The Impact of GenAI Literacy on Consumer Decision-Making: A Moderated Mediation Model of Information Overload and Consumer Involvement
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of consumer decision-making by providing unprecedented levels of personalized information. However, the inherent complexity and potential for AI hallucinations introduce significant cognitive challenges that may undermine decision quality. Grounded in Information Processing Theory (IPT), this study investigates the mechanism through which GenAI literacy influences consumer decision quality, specifically focusing on the mediating role of perceived information overload and the moderating role of consumer involvement. Through a structured survey of 401 Chinese college students and subsequent structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis, the empirical results demonstrate that GenAI literacy is directly and positively associated with decision quality. Furthermore, perceived information overload serves as a critical mediator, indicating that high levels of GenAI literacy could reduce cognitive friction and prevent decision paralysis. Notably, the continuous latent interaction analysis reveals that consumer involvement significantly moderates the relationship between GenAI literacy and perceived information overload, with the inhibitory effect of literacy being more pronounced in high-involvement scenarios. These findings extend the application of IPT to the era of human-AI symbiosis and offer actionable insights for policymakers and enterprises to optimize the digital consumption ecosystem.

item.title: How AI Is Transforming Education: Toward a Symbiotic Relationship among AI, Teachers, and Students
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping education by reorganizing interactions among teaching, learning, and instructional decision-making. Existing research has largely focused on isolated tools or specific learning outcomes, providing limited insight into how AI operates within integrated educational systems. This study examines an AI-enabled educational environment to explore how interactions among AI systems, teachers, and students relate to changes in instructional organization and student performance. Drawing on multi-source data generated from routine teaching activities, the findings suggest overall improvements in learning outcomes and indicate three interconnected mechanisms: improved instructional efficiency through reduced routine workload, stronger alignment between diagnosis and feedback, and a complementary division of roles between human teachers and AI systems. By linking learning outcomes with underlying instructional processes, the study provides system-level evidence on how integrated AI-enabled environments reshape educational practice and contribute to the emerging symbiotic relationship among AI, teachers, and students.

item.title: Institutional digitalization and digital stress: a four-wave observational study of teacher-reported AI-collaborative teaching in physical education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction How institutional digitalization relates to teachers’ experience of work and subsequent artificial intelligence (AI)-supported practice remains unclear. Methods Drawing on job demands-resources principles, we examined these relationships in a four-wave observational cohort of 961 physical education teachers from 120 Chinese institutions. We linked an organizational-source digitalization proxy to teacher questionnaires and a study-specific teacher-reported score of AI involvement in teaching tasks. Analyses adjusted for baseline practice and separated between-institution from teacher-relative associations. Results Two of five primary tests met the Holm-adjusted criterion. The stress-related product of between-institution coefficients was negative (−0.099; pointwise 95% confidence interval [−0.184, −0.033]). The positive digitalization–stress association was weaker among teachers with higher digital self-efficacy relative to colleagues (interaction coefficient −0.101; [−0.168, −0.037]) but remained positive at the low, average, and high self-efficacy levels examined. The adjusted digitalization–practice association, appraisal-related coefficient product, and appraisal interaction did not meet the corrected criterion. Discussion The findings connect the organization and experience of work with reported AI practice, emphasizing perceived digital work pressure and relative self-efficacy while complementing accounts centered on technology acceptance.

item.title: Artificial intelligence and its influence on student engagement in higher education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Empirical evidence on how artificial intelligence (AI) relates to student engagement in culturally diverse higher-education settings remains limited. In Chinese university classrooms, where interaction is often teacher-led and asking questions in class can carry a social cost, AI-driven dialogic tools may offer low-pressure opportunities for active participation. This study examined the association between an AI conversational agent (EduBot) and the behavioural, cognitive, emotional and agentic dimensions of engagement among Chinese undergraduates. A mixed-methods quasi-experimental design involved 555 students in four comprehensive (multi-disciplinary, research-intensive) universities, each contributing one introductory course taught in two parallel sections. Within a 15-week semester, intervention sections (n = 278) used EduBot, a Socratic-dialogue agent embedded in the learning management system, for 12 weeks; control sections (n = 277) used teaching-assistant-moderated forums. We measured engagement at three time points with a 21-item four-dimensional engagement scale adapted from an established measure and supplemented it with system logs, 30 student interviews and instructor focus groups. Linear mixed-effects models accounting for the nesting of students within course sections, together with mixed-design ANOVAs, showed Group × Time interactions for behavioural (η 2 p = 0.043, post-test d = 0.71), cognitive (η 2 p = 0.032, d = 0.55), agentic (η 2 p = 0.054, d = 0.57) and emotional engagement (η 2 p = 0.012, d = 0.34), all p ≤ 0.001 after Holm adjustment. Within the intervention group, the number of EduBot sessions predicted post-test engagement after adjustment for baseline scores and covariates. Exploratory moderation analyses indicated larger agentic gains among first-year students and larger cognitive gains among students with lower prior GPA. Thematic analysis identified three hypothesised mechanisms, namely a judgment-free interaction space, scaffolded persistence and temporal flexibility. A Socratic-scaffolded AI agent was associated with higher engagement, most clearly for agentic engagement, which participants described as constrained by classroom norms. The findings support culturally attentive AI design and suggest, tentatively, an equity-enhancing potential. Because the design compared an integrated AI package with usual practice across eight sections, the effects cannot be attributed to single design components.

item.title: Intelligent scaffolding for musical practice: a systematic review of AI and digital support for the self-regulated learning cycle
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Independent music practice depends on learners’ self-regulated learning (SRL), yet how digital tools and artificial intelligence (AI) support the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases of the SRL cycle, and when such support may undermine learner autonomy, remains unclear. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we searched Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PsycINFO through March 2026. Sixteen empirical studies met the inclusion criteria and were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Because of methodological heterogeneity, we conducted a thematic synthesis rather than a meta-analysis. Results Three categories emerged: traditional digital tools, discriminative AI, and generative AI. Traditional tools supported planning and reflection; discriminative AI enabled real-time error detection; and generative AI may help learners manage task difficulty and translate expert feedback into actionable steps. Study quality was uneven, and several findings came from small-sample or cross-sectional designs, which limits causal inference. Two potential risks, over-scaffolding that may diminish autonomy and visual feedback that may divert attention from sound, were insufficiently studied. Discussion Digital and AI tools appear to scaffold different phases of SRL, but learner autonomy should remain at the core. Fading explicit support and pedagogical guidance may help reduce dependence. Longitudinal studies are required to test these mechanisms.

item.title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.
